target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is ethically acceptable because most specimens are already deceased or are meat-industry byproducts
objection: AG2 argues that, in practice, the vast majority of dissection animals are caught in the wild, which harms local populations and biodiversity; therefore, the sourcing is not ethically benign.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is necessary or required for biology/medical education
objection: AG2 says dissection is not required by the AP Biology framework or the Next Generation Science Standards, and no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals for physician training, so it is not an essential educational requirement.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection teaches better than alternatives
objection: AG2 contends that synthetic models, 3D software, interactive simulations, and high-quality videos teach equally well or better while avoiding animal death, variability, and other downsides.

target: AG1’s claim that hands-on learning requires real animal dissection
objection: AG2 says students can still practice measurement, observation, and technique with non-animal materials, so the hands-on learning benefit does not depend on killing animals.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is mainly harmless because specimens are byproducts or already dead
objection: AG2 argues that even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection still creates chemical and waste harms: preservatives like formaldehyde/formalin, biohazardous waste, and disposal burdens that alternatives avoid.

target: AG1’s claim that educational value justifies making students participate in dissection
objection: AG2 objects that dissection can exclude or burden students with ethical, religious, or personal objections, and that the most inclusive approach is to replace dissection with animal-free alternatives rather than rely on opt-outs.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct sourcing solves the ethical problem
objection: AG2 says using byproducts does not justify a system that still normalizes an animal procurement and processing pipeline for education when non-animal methods can meet the same goals.

target: AG1’s claim that safety regulations and waste procedures make dissection acceptable
objection: AG2 responds that regulation does not eliminate the underlying harms of hazardous preservatives and regulated chemical/bio waste, and that safer handling still leaves dissection worse than effective non-animal alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-outs and accommodations solve the inclusion problem
objection: AG2 argues that if dissection remains the default activity, students who object still face pressure, stigma, or extra accommodation burdens; the more inclusive solution is to replace dissection as the centerpiece.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct sourcing makes animal dissection acceptable
objection: AG2 says that even when some specimens are byproducts, the practice still normalizes animal killing/processing for educational purposes, which is unnecessary if models and simulations work.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be an equity tool because not all schools can afford advanced alternatives
objection: AG2 counters that dissection itself creates inequities and harms: some students get alternatives while all students absorb environmental and chemical impacts, so equity is not just about access to tactile experience.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives cannot be scaled as practically as dissection
objection: AG2 says alternatives are reusable across cohorts, while dissection requires recurring purchases and disposal of preserved biological waste and chemicals, making non-animal methods more practical over time.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can reliably require responsibly sourced byproduct specimens
objection: AG2 argues that conditional sourcing is hard to verify consistently in real school settings, so the best-case sourcing scenario cannot justify keeping dissection as a norm.

target: AG1’s proposal to make dissection opt-in while keeping it available
objection: AG2 says opt-in is not real consent in school settings because students can still face pressure from grading, lab scheduling, supply constraints, and social stigma; therefore, opt-in does not remove the ethical problem.

target: AG1’s claim that a small amount of dissection is acceptable if it uses already-deceased/byproduct specimens and good procedures
objection: AG2 responds that if non-animal methods meet the same learning goals, then any remaining animal dissection is still an ethically inferior and unnecessary practice.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely trains real lab skills and safety habits
objection: AG2 says those generic lab skills—PPE use, tool handling, measurement, observation, contamination control—can be taught just as effectively with synthetic models and non-animal substrates, so the animal body itself is unnecessary.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct sourcing avoids moral problems
objection: AG2 argues that byproducts still come from an animal supply chain with welfare and environmental impacts, so dissection remains tied to the broader animal-harm problem.

target: AG1’s claim that policy design can eliminate coercion from opt-in dissection
objection: AG2 says school scheduling, limited materials, staffing differences, and grading practices vary too much for policy alone to reliably remove pressure; dissection remains a default that can coerce participation.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is morally acceptable if sourcing is byproduct-based and harms are incremental
objection: AG2 says contract-based sourcing cannot reliably guarantee that there is no upstream animal harm or supply-chain expansion, so the best-case procurement story cannot justify keeping dissection as a normal option.

target: AG1’s claim that “incremental harm” is acceptable because dissection is a harm-reducing use of material
objection: AG2 answers that any avoidable harm still matters when effective non-animal methods exist, so choosing animal bodies is not proportionate to educational need.

target: AG1’s autonomy argument that a ban overrides the choices of students and teachers who want real specimens
objection: AG2 says respecting autonomy does not justify requiring animal bodies as an option; a pro-student-rights policy should avoid making dissection the default learning method at all.

target: AG1’s claim that students can be protected from pressure through truly optional dissection
objection: AG2 argues that even with no grading penalty and separate scheduling, students who object can still experience stigma and coercion-by-practice, so the default pressure problem remains.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be framed as responsible use and stewardship
objection: AG2 says that curriculum framing cannot remove the underlying moral tradeoff: the activity still depends on animal bodies, and if alternatives teach the same biology, the school should not require students to learn that way.

target: AG1’s claim that real anatomy may strengthen empathy and ethical understanding
objection: AG2 responds that teaching humane science does not require the practice itself; ethics can be taught through case studies, sourcing discussions, and non-animal materials without using animal bodies.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should remain because ethics can be taught through reflective practice alongside it
objection: AG2 argues that ethical reflection does not remove the underlying harm tradeoff, and may even backfire by normalizing the idea that using animal bodies for learning is acceptable.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s value justifies keeping it as an option when alternatives exist
objection: AG2 invokes a precaution/avoidance principle: when effective alternatives already achieve the curriculum goals, schools should avoid an activity with uncertain but real animal and environmental downsides.

target: AG1’s claim that distress from dissection can be handled by accommodation and age-appropriate design
objection: AG2 says dissection can still impose predictable psychological and developmental harms on minors, including distress from smell, visuals, and handling animal tissue, which alternatives avoid entirely.

target: AG1’s claim that age-appropriate or less-graphic dissection solves the problem
objection: AG2 contends that making dissections less graphic or more curated undermines the supposed unique value of the practice and makes it look like a more artificial exposure that alternatives can do just as well.
